t: a > 0: minimum point; a < 0: maximum point.

nota.t: A quadratic function has the form f(x) = ax² + bx + c, with a ≠ 0 and highest power 2. Its graph is a parabola: opening upwards if a > 0 (minimum point), downwards if a < 0 (maximum point). The axis of symmetry is x = −b/2a. A quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 is solved by factorising; the roots are the x-intercepts.

t: Write in general form ax² + bx + c = 0
Base b: place values 1, b, b², b³ ...

nota.t: A number base sets how many digits are used: base 2 (0, 1), base 5 (0–4), base 8 (0–7), base 10 (0–9). Place values are powers of the base: …, b², b¹, b⁰. Convert to base 10 by multiplying each digit by its place value; convert from base 10 by repeated division.

t: If p, then q. Converse: if q, then p. Inverse: if not p, then not q. Contrapositive: if not q, then not p.
Deductive: general → specific. Inductive: specific → general.

nota.t: An argument has premises and a conclusion. Deductive arguments draw a specific conclusion from a general premise; inductive arguments draw a general conclusion from specific cases. Valid forms: Form I (All A are B; C is A; so C is B), Form II (If p then q; p; so q) and Form III (If p then q; not q; so not p).
Form II: If it rains, the road is wet. It is raining. So the road is wet.

A statement is a sentence that is true or false but not both. Quantifiers: 'all' and 'some'. Negation 'not p' changes the truth value. 'p and q' is true only if both are true; 'p or q' is false only if both are false. An implication 'if p, then q' has a converse (if q, then p), inverse (if not p, then not q) and contrapositive (if not q, then not p).
Implication: If x = 3, then x² = 9 (true). Converse: If x² = 9, then x = 3 (false, x could be −3).

t: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

nota.t: The intersection A ∩ B is the set of elements in both A and B. On a Venn diagram it is the overlapping region. The complement (A ∩ B)′ is every element of ξ not in A ∩ B.
The union A ∪ B is the set of all elements in A or B or both. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
Example: 25 like football, 18 like badminton, 7 like both. n(A ∪ B) = 25 + 18 − 7 = 36.
Combined operations such as A ∪ (B ∩ C) or (A ∪ B)′ ∩ C are done brackets first. Shade the regions on the Venn diagram step by step.

A network is a graph of vertices joined by edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges meeting it; sum of degrees = 2 × number of edges. Directed graphs have arrows; weighted graphs carry values (distance, cost, time) on edges. A tree has no cycles; networks are used to find shortest routes.
Example: a graph with 5 vertices and 7 edges → sum of degrees = 14.

t: Solid line: ≤ or ≥. Dashed line: < or >.
Test a point to find the region.

nota.t: A system of linear inequalities has two or more inequalities; its solution is the region satisfying all of them at once. It is used for problems such as planning production under constraints.

t: Test a point to choose the side

nota.t: A linear inequality in two variables such as y ≤ 2x + 1 is shown as a region on a graph. Use a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >. The region above the line satisfies y > mx + c; below satisfies y < mx + c.
A speed-time graph shows speed against time. Gradient = acceleration (negative means deceleration). The area under the graph = distance travelled. A horizontal line means uniform speed.
Example: 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s, then steady for 20 s. Distance = ½(10)(20) + 20(20) = 500 m.
A distance-time graph shows distance from the start against time. Gradient = speed. A horizontal line means the object is at rest. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
Example: 120 km in 2 h, stop 30 min, then 60 km in 1 h. Average speed = 180 ÷ 3.5 = 51.4 km/h.

topik.nama: 8. Measures of Dispersion for Ungrouped Data

t: Range, interquartile range, variance, standard deviation.

nota.t: Dispersion shows how spread out data are. Two data sets can share a mean but differ in spread. Data can be shown as dot plots, stem-and-leaf plots and box plots.

Measures of dispersion for ungrouped data: range (largest − smallest), interquartile range (Q₃ − Q₁), variance σ² = Σx²/N − x̄² and standard deviation σ = √variance. A box plot shows minimum, Q₁, median, Q₃ and maximum; outliers are extreme values.

t: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

nota.t: 9.3 Mutually Exclusive and Non-Mutually Exclusive Events
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For non-mutually exclusive events: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
Example: cards 1–10. A = even, B = multiple of 3. P(A ∪ B) = 5/10 + 3/10 − 1/10 = 7/10.
Independent events: one outcome does not affect the other, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Dependent events: the first outcome affects the second, such as drawing marbles without replacement.
Example: 5 red, 3 blue, two marbles without replacement. P(red, red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 5/14.
A combined event involves two or more events. The sample space is listed with a list, table or tree diagram.

v.c: Part of the sample space for a dice and a coin

nota.t: Probability of combined events supports decisions, such as the chance of passing two tests or two machines failing. Tree diagrams help with multi-stage probabilities.
Example: P(pass test 1) = 0.8, P(pass test 2) = 0.7 (independent). P(pass both) = 0.56.

t: SMART goals, cash flow, fixed and variable expenses.

nota.t: Financial planning: set SMART goals, review your finances, make a plan (budget), carry it out and review it. A budget lists income, fixed and variable expenses and savings (at least 10% is advised). Separate needs from wants.
Example: income RM3 000. Save 20% = RM600; surplus = income − expenses − savings.
